planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep in humus-rich, sharply drained soil; mulch roots to keep them cool even though top growth takes full sun.

directions: Collected by French missionary-naturalist Armand David in the mountains of Sichuan, this wild Turk's-cap lily sends up slender, leafy stems topped with several nodding, strongly recurved flowers in brick-orange to scarlet, heavily freckled with maroon spots. It blooms in midsummer on wiry stems that hold up well without staking, and the narrow grassy leaves give the plant an airy, wildflower look distinct from showier hybrid lilies. This species was one of the parents used to breed early Asiatic hybrid strains, but the true wild form is still collected and offered by specialty lily growers and seed exchanges for its grace in a naturalistic border. Give it good winter drainage, since rot rather than cold is what typically kills it.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil with roots shaded and flowering stems reaching toward sun; benefits from a loose woodland-edge mulch.

directions: Native to open woodland and scrub in Sichuan and Yunnan, this is one of the wild Chinese trumpet lilies behind vintage hybrid strains such as 'Black Dragon.' Tall stems carry a handful of long, flaring, creamy-white trumpets with a yellow throat and a wash of maroon-purple on the reverse of the petals, opening from dark buds in midsummer with a strong, sweet fragrance. It performs best with its base in cool, humus-rich shade and its flowering stems reaching into brighter light, mimicking its native woodland-margin habitat. Specialty lily and bulb growers still offer true seed-grown stock of the wild species, distinct from the many garden hybrids derived from it.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in gritty, fast-draining soil or an alpine trough; needs a hot, dry summer rest to replicate its native Anatolian scree habitat.

directions: A diminutive alpine fritillary from limestone screes in central Anatolia, Turkey, producing a single nodding, glossy golden-yellow bell with faint bronze tessellation inside the petals. Its low stature and early spring bloom make it a favorite for rock gardens, raised beds, and alpine troughs where its understated color can be appreciated up close. Like most high-altitude Turkish fritillaries, it demands sharp winter and spring drainage followed by a baked, bone-dry summer dormancy, conditions readily achieved in a scree bed or pot under glass. It is a regular offering from alpine bulb specialists and rock-garden society seed exchanges.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (NARGS) seed exchange

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in gritty, humus-rich soil on a sunny bank or in open woodland scrub, mimicking its native limestone garrigue habitat.

directions: This southern French and northwestern Italian species grows wild in limestone garrigue and open scrub of Provence and Liguria, where it is distinguished from its relatives by a leafy whorl of bracts surrounding the solitary nodding flower. Blooms are pale green to cream, heavily netted with purple-brown tessellation, opening in early spring on wiry stems among narrow gray-green leaves. It is less commonly grown than the Pyrenean fritillaries but is sought by Mediterranean bulb collectors and offered occasionally through specialty alpine nurseries and bulb society seed lists. Give it a hot, dry summer rest after the foliage dies back to mimic its native Mediterranean climate.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4 inches deep in well-drained soil in a sunny border or rock garden; very cold-tolerant and does not need the extreme summer baking some Mediterranean fritillaries require.

directions: Ranging from the steppes of Eastern Europe and southern Russia into Central Asia, this cold-hardy fritillary carries one to several nodding, deep maroon-brown bells netted with fine tessellation, held above whorled leaves whose uppermost pair often ends in a thin coiling tendril. It blooms in early to mid spring and tolerates considerably more winter cold and clay-adjacent soils than many of its Mediterranean relatives, making it an easier entry point for growers new to species fritillaries. Clumps increase slowly by offsets and self-sown seed in favorable sites. It is a steady presence on rock-garden society seed exchange lists and is carried by a handful of specialty bulb nurseries.
sources: North American Rock Garden Society (NARGS) seed exchange

planting.note: Plant small bulbs 3 inches deep in sharply drained soil in a sunny rock garden, raised bed, or alpine pot; wants a dry summer rest after its very early spring bloom.

directions: Native to rocky slopes in the Pamir-Alai and western Tian Shan ranges of Central Asia, this tiny fritillary pushes up several narrow, tubular, bell-shaped flowers striped in soft pink and white along a short stem, often appearing while snow is still nearby in very early spring. Its diminutive size and early flowering make it a prized subject for alpine troughs, raised scree beds, and cold frames among specialist bulb growers. Because it comes from a region with a sharp, dry continental climate, it needs excellent winter drainage and a thoroughly dry, baked dormancy through summer. Seed and occasional bulb stock circulate through Central Asian bulb specialists and bulb society seed exchanges.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade; naturally compact wild forms need no pruning to stay low and spreading.

directions: Found on rocky cliffs and mountain slopes across Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu in Japan, this species ranges from low, mat-forming dwarf populations to taller upright shrubs depending on provenance, so wild-collected or seed-grown stock varies in habit more than named dwarf selections do. Clear pale-yellow flowers, sometimes blushed with green, open in trusses of several blooms in mid-spring against small, glossy, leathery leaves that often take on bronze tones in cold weather. It is one of the hardier yellow-flowered rhododendron species available to temperate gardeners and tolerates more open exposure than many Asian species once established. True species seed, as opposed to the popular dwarf cultivar selections derived from it, is distributed through the American Rhododendron Society seed exchange.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, acidic, sharply drained soil in a sunny rock garden; dislikes soggy winter ground more than it dislikes cold or wind.

directions: Native to open, exposed alpine meadows and scree at high elevation in Yunnan and Sichuan, China, this is one of the smallest rhododendron species in general cultivation, forming a dense, twiggy mound of tiny gray-green leaves rarely more than a foot tall. In mid-spring it disappears almost entirely under small, flat, violet-blue to purple flowers that nearly cover the foliage. Because it grows naturally on open, well-drained alpine ground, it tolerates far more direct sun and wind than most woodland rhododendron species, making it a staple of rock gardens and trough plantings. It has also been used as a parent of several popular dwarf blue-flowered rhododendron cultivars, though the wild species itself remains in specialty and rock-garden nursery trade.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, peaty, well-drained soil in a cool, partly shaded rock garden or trough; appreciates a mulch of grit or fine bark around the crown.

directions: Native to high alpine pastures and rocky ledges of Yunnan and northern Myanmar, this is among the lowest-growing rhododendron species in cultivation, forming a tight, ground-hugging carpet of small, rounded, aromatic leaves. In late spring it produces disproportionately large, waxy, bell-shaped flowers held just above the foliage, varying by wild population from pale pink through plum-purple to near-black maroon. Its naturally prostrate habit suits it to trough gardens, raised beds, and the fronts of rock gardens where larger rhododendrons would overwhelm the planting. Specialty rhododendron nurseries and the American Rhododendron Society seed exchange both offer true species stock alongside its better-known named color forms.
